body: Every long-run winner in this library had at least one deep drawdown: Amazon -94% (1999-2001), Booking -99% (2000-02), MercadoLibre ~-88% (2008) and ~-67% (2021-22), Netflix ~-80% (2011-12) and -76% (2021-22), Shopify -87% (2022), Meta -77% (2021-22), Palantir -87% (2021-22), Apple -61% (2007-09) and -44% (2012-13), Microsoft -37% (2022), AMD -67% (2021-22), TSMC -58% (2022), ASML -59% (2021-22). Recovery signal that was visible at the bottom in the cases that recovered: core engagement/usage metrics kept growing (Netflix streaming hours, Meta daily users, MELI payments volume) and the cause was management choices or macro, not loss of the moat; management then made a visible reversal (Netflix dropping Qwikster, Meta's efficiency cuts, Shopify selling logistics). Non-recoveries in this set (SMCI, Enphase, Novo so far) had moat or governance problems instead: commodity margins, subsidy-dependent demand, or a superior competitor. Practical rules: size positions so a -75% move is survivable (see strategy:position-sizing); write down in advance which usage metric would prove the business, not the stock, is broken.

data.rule: track usage metric vs price; size for -75%

title: Great businesses crash -75% too: separate the broken stock from the broken business

body: Apr-2026 memo (published 9 Apr 2026): private equity returns have 'fallen precipitously' (MSCI estimate cited: US PE funds ~5.8% annualised 2022-Q3 2025 vs 11.6% for the S&P 500); future private-loan performance depends on sponsor skill and on exits; weak borrowers increasingly use payment-in-kind (PIK) interest instead of cash service. Lenders' security comes from borrower performance and seniority; disciplined underwriters will be fine. Marks closes by quoting Oaktree's Bob O'Leary comparing today to the high-yield bust of 1989-91: a new instrument over-indulged, then spooked by a Middle East war - 'Ultimately, high yield was fine (even great), and direct lending will be as well, but it may have to go through a credit cycle to get to a better place.' Sep-2026 'Part III' memo: 'you can't ignore the laws of economics and expect to come out ahead'; the US cannot 'perpetually spend more than it takes in' without its 'currency and Treasury securities' being 'disrespected'; but selling US stocks is not the answer since dollar cash and bonds carry the same risk, and non-US assets bring 'other risks' (slower growth, regulation, EM uncertainty). Modest diversification makes sense for 'investors with non-dollar needs.' Actionable for an Indian investor: rising PIK share is a stress signal in any credit book (including Indian NBFC/AIF credit); US fiscal risk argues for INR-based core holdings with only considered USD diversification.
title: Marks 2026 on private credit ('What's Going On in Private Credit?', Apr) and US fiscal risk ('Repeal the Laws of Economics III', Sep)
